diagrams.title: Patterns the big apps share
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  a["Start as a monolith, split along team and domain lines"] --> b["Cache aggressively: CDN, Redis, in-process"]
  b --> c["Asynchronous by default: queues and events"]
  c --> d["Partition data by user / tenant / region"]
  d --> e["Design for failure: retries, circuit breakers, chaos testing"]
  e --> f["Measure everything: SLOs drive priorities"]
diagrams.explain: Amazon, Instagram, Netflix, Slack, Stripe and Uber arrived at the same habits independently: grow out of a monolith rather than starting with dozens of services, cache at every layer, move work off the request path, partition data so no single machine holds everything, assume components fail, and let measured service levels — not guesses — decide what to fix next.

sections.title: 1. Amazon
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- 300M+ active customers
- Millions of orders per day
- Black Friday: 100x normal traffic in minutes
- Sub-100ms page load requirement

### Architecture Evolution

```
2001: Monolith (single Oracle DB)
      ↓ Could not scale. Deployments took hours.
2004: Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)
      ↓ Each team owns a service with its own database
2010: Microservices (thousands of independent services)
      ↓ API Gateway routes to correct service
2020: Serverless + Event-Driven (Lambda, EventBridge)
```

### Key Decisions & Lessons

**1. Two-Pizza Team Rule**

- Each microservice owned by a team small enough to feed with two pizzas
- Teams deploy independently (10,000+ deployments per day)
- **Takeaway**: Design services small enough for one team to own end-to-end

**2. Database-Per-Service (No shared databases)**

```
Order Service → Orders DB (DynamoDB)
Product Service → Product DB (Aurora PostgreSQL)
User Service → User DB (DynamoDB)
Inventory Service → Inventory DB (DynamoDB)
```

- Services communicate via APIs and events, NEVER by sharing a database
- **Takeaway**: Shared databases create coupling that prevents independent scaling

**3. Eventually Consistent (Not ACID Everywhere)**

```
When you click "Buy":
1. Order Service → Creates order (status: pending)
2. Publishes "OrderCreated" event
3. Payment Service → Charges card → Publishes "PaymentCompleted"
4. Inventory Service → Reserves stock → Publishes "StockReserved"
5. Order Service → Updates status to "confirmed"

If payment fails → Compensating transaction (cancel order, release stock)
```

- **Takeaway**: At Amazon's scale, distributed transactions (2PC) are too slow. Use the Saga pattern.

**4. Caching Everything**

- ElastiCache (Redis) for session data, product catalog cache
- CloudFront CDN for static assets (images, JS, CSS)
- DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for database query caching
- **Takeaway**: Cache aggressively. Every millisecond of latency = revenue lost.

### How This Maps to Your Projects

- **Project 2 (E-Commerce)**: You built the same patterns — separate DBs for products (MongoDB) and orders (PostgreSQL), Redis caching, event-driven order processing with Celery.

sections.title: 2. Instagram
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- 2B+ monthly active users
- 100M+ photos uploaded daily
- News Feed must load in < 1 second
- Global distribution (every country)

### Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Load Balancer (DNS-based)               │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           │
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│                    Django (Python) API                    │
│  - Yes, Instagram runs on Python/Django                  │
│  - Async workers with Celery                             │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                           │
    ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
    │                      │                      │
┌───▼───────┐   ┌─────────▼────────┐   ┌────────▼──────┐
│PostgreSQL │   │ Cassandra        │   │ Redis          │
│(users,    │   │(news feed,       │   │(sessions,      │
│ relations)│   │ activities)      │   │ caching,       │
│           │   │                  │   │ rate limits)   │
└───────────┘   └──────────────────┘   └───────────────┘
```

### Key Decisions & Lessons

**1. Fan-Out on Write (Pre-computed Feeds)**

```
When @katyperry posts a photo (400M followers):
  Problem: Cannot fan-out to 400M followers in real time

Solution: Hybrid approach
  - Celebrity posts → Fan-out on READ (lazy loading)
  - Regular users  → Fan-out on WRITE (pre-computed)

When regular user posts:
  1. Celery task gets all follower IDs from PostgreSQL
  2. For each follower, LPUSH post_id to their feed in Redis
  3. When follower opens app, read their pre-computed feed from Redis
```

- **Takeaway**: Fan-out on write is faster for reads but expensive for users with millions of followers. Use hybrid.

**2. PostgreSQL at Scale**

- Instagram is one of the largest PostgreSQL deployments in the world
- Sharded across dozens of PostgreSQL instances
- pgbouncer for connection pooling (thousands of connections per shard)
- **Takeaway**: PostgreSQL can scale to billions of rows with proper sharding and connection pooling

**3. Celery for Everything Async**

- Photo processing, feed fan-out, notifications, analytics
- Thousands of Celery workers processing millions of tasks/hour
- **Takeaway**: Offload anything that doesn't need an immediate response to background workers

### How This Maps to Your Projects

- **Project 3 (Social Media)**: You built the exact fan-out pattern with Redis, Celery for async processing, and PostgreSQL for the social graph.

sections.title: 3. ChatGPT
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- 100M+ weekly active users (fastest growing app ever)
- Each request: 10-60 seconds of GPU computation
- Streaming responses (token by token)
- Conversation context management
- Multi-model serving (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o)

### Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Client (Browser/Mobile)                     │
│  SSE Connection → Receives tokens as they're generated       │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐
│                   API Gateway + Rate Limiter                  │
│  - Per-user rate limits based on subscription tier            │
│  - Free: 3 msgs/min, Plus: 40 msgs/3hr, Team: higher        │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Inference Router                            │
│  - Routes to correct model cluster (GPT-4, 4o, etc.)         │
│  - Load balances across GPU pools                            │
│  - Queue management during high traffic                      │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
    ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
    │                      │                      │
┌───▼───────────┐  ┌──────▼──────────┐  ┌───────▼─────────┐
│ GPT-4o Pool   │  │ GPT-4 Pool      │  │ GPT-3.5 Pool    │
│ (A100 GPUs)   │  │ (A100 GPUs)     │  │ (A10 GPUs)      │
│ Lower latency │  │ Higher quality   │  │ Fast + cheap     │
└───────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘
```

### Key Decisions & Lessons

**1. Server-Sent Events (SSE) for Streaming**

```
Why SSE and not WebSockets?
- SSE is simpler (unidirectional: server → client)
- Works over standard HTTP (no upgrade needed)
- Automatic reconnection built into browsers
- ChatGPT only needs server-to-client streaming

Response format:
data: {"id":"chatcmpl-abc","choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Hello"}}]}
data: {"id":"chatcmpl-abc","choices":[{"delta":{"content":" world"}}]}
data: [DONE]
```

- **Takeaway**: Use SSE when you only need server-to-client streaming. WebSockets are overkill for this.

**2. Conversation Storage**

```
Conversations stored in database (likely PostgreSQL + blob storage):
- Conversation metadata: PostgreSQL
- Message history: Likely a document store or blob
- NOT stored in model memory — full context sent with each request

Each API call sends the FULL conversation:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is Python?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Python is a programming..."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Show me an example"},  # New message
]
```

- **Takeaway**: LLMs are stateless. The application manages conversation history and sends full context each time.

**3. Request Queuing Under Load**

- When GPU clusters are full, requests are queued
- Users see "ChatGPT is at capacity" or experience slower responses
- Priority queue: Paid users get priority over free users
- **Takeaway**: For expensive operations, implement request queuing with priority tiers.

### How This Maps to Your Projects

- **Project 4 (ChatGPT Clone)**: You built SSE streaming, conversation management in MongoDB, per-tier rate limiting, and multi-model support.

sections.title: 4. Claude (Anthropic)
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- Similar to ChatGPT but with focus on safety/alignment
- 200K token context window (massive memory per request)
- Tool use (function calling) requires orchestration
- Streaming with thinking/reasoning display

### Key Technical Differences from ChatGPT

**1. Massive Context Window Management**

```
Claude's 200K context = ~150K words = a full novel

Challenge: Processing 200K tokens uses significant GPU memory
Solution:
- Context caching (if same system prompt, reuse KV cache)
- Sliding window attention for very long contexts
- Prompt caching at API level (cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"})

API cost optimization:
- Cached input tokens: $0.30 / MTok (90% cheaper)
- Regular input tokens: $3.00 / MTok
```

**2. Extended Thinking (Reasoning Display)**

```
Claude shows its reasoning process:

Response structure:
{
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "thinking",
      "thinking": "Let me analyze this step by step..."
    },
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "The answer is 42."
    }
  ]
}

Streamed as separate content blocks — UI renders thinking in collapsible section
```

**3. Tool Use Architecture**

```
1. User asks: "What's the weather in Tokyo?"
2. Claude responds with tool_use block: {"name": "get_weather", "input": {"city": "Tokyo"}}
3. Application executes the function
4. Application sends tool_result back to Claude
5. Claude generates final response incorporating the result

This is the agentic pattern you built in Project 5 (RAG SaaS) with LangGraph!
```

### How This Maps to Your Projects

- **Project 4 & 5**: Multi-model support, streaming, and tool-use agentic patterns.

sections.title: 5. Netflix
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- 250M+ subscribers in 190 countries
- 17,000+ titles, personalized per user
- Video must start in < 2 seconds
- Adaptive bitrate for varying network conditions

### Key Decisions

**1. Microservice Decomposition**

- 1000+ microservices
- Each service owns its data (DynamoDB, Cassandra, MySQL)
- Services communicate via gRPC and async events

**2. Edge Computing (Open Connect CDN)**

```
Netflix CDN:
- 17,000+ servers in ISP data centers worldwide
- 95% of video traffic served from edge (not from AWS)
- When you press play, video comes from a server
  possibly in your ISP's building

Content preparation:
1. New movie uploaded → Transcoded into 1200+ versions
   (different resolutions, codecs, audio tracks, subtitles)
2. Versions distributed to edge servers based on predicted demand
3. Popular content pre-positioned at more edge locations
```

**3. Chaos Engineering (Chaos Monkey)**

- Netflix randomly kills production servers to test resilience
- If your system survives random failures, it's truly fault-tolerant
- **Takeaway**: Design for failure. Every service should handle downstream failures gracefully.

### How This Maps to Your Projects

- **Project 8 (Video Streaming)**: You built HLS adaptive streaming, multi-resolution transcoding, and CDN delivery patterns.

sections.title: 6. Slack
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- 32M+ daily active users
- Millions of messages per second
- Real-time delivery (< 100ms)
- Multi-device synchronization
- Workspace (tenant) isolation

### Key Architecture

```
WebSocket Gateway (persistent connections)
    │
    ├─ Message Service → MySQL (messages) + Search (Elasticsearch)
    ├─ Presence Service → Redis (who's online)
    ├─ Channel Service → MySQL (channels, members)
    └─ File Service → S3 (file uploads)
```

**Real-Time Delivery**: WebSocket connections to every client. When you send a message, it's written to MySQL, then broadcast via WebSocket to all channel members.

**Multi-Tenant**: Each Slack workspace is a tenant. Data is sharded by workspace ID.

### How This Maps to Your Projects

- **Project 6 (Real-Time Chat)**: WebSocket with Redis Pub/Sub, presence tracking, typing indicators.
- **Project 10 (Multi-Tenant SaaS)**: Workspace isolation, per-tenant data.

sections.title: 7. Stripe
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- Process billions in payments annually
- 99.999% uptime requirement (< 5 minutes downtime/year)
- PCI DSS compliance (payment security)
- Idempotent operations (no double charges)

### Key Lessons

**1. Idempotency Keys**

```python
# Every Stripe API call accepts an idempotency key
stripe.PaymentIntent.create(
    amount=2000,
    currency="usd",
    idempotency_key="order_12345_payment_attempt_1"
)
# If network fails and you retry with same key → same result, no double charge
```

**2. Event-Driven with Webhooks**

```
Payment flow:
1. Create PaymentIntent → Returns client_secret
2. Client confirms payment (3D Secure, etc.)
3. Stripe sends webhook: payment_intent.succeeded
4. Your server fulfills the order

Why webhooks? Because payment can take minutes (bank auth, 3D Secure).
Never poll. Always use webhooks for async payment events.
```

### How This Maps to Your Projects

- **Project 2 (E-Commerce)**: Stripe integration, webhook handling, idempotent order creation.

sections.title: 8. Uber
sections.body:
### The Challenge

- Match riders with drivers in real-time
- Location updates every 4 seconds from millions of drivers
- Price calculation (surge pricing) at massive scale
- Global operation across 10,000+ cities

### Key Architecture

**Geospatial Indexing**

```
Instead of: SELECT * FROM drivers WHERE distance(lat, lng) < 5km
            (scans every driver — O(n))

Uber uses: Google S2 Geometry library
           Divides Earth into hierarchical cells
           Query: "Give me all drivers in cell XYZ"
           Covered by index — O(log n)
```

**CQRS for Supply/Demand**

```
Write path: Driver location updates → Kafka → Location DB
Read path:  "Find nearby drivers" → Pre-computed geospatial index (Redis)

Separated because:
- Writes: Millions per second (every driver, every 4 seconds)
- Reads: Thousands per second (rider requests)
- Different scaling needs
```

sections.title: Key Patterns Summary
sections.body:
| Pattern               | Used By               | When to Use                                   |
| --------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| **Microservices**     | Amazon, Netflix, Uber | When teams need independent deployment        |
| **SSE Streaming**     | ChatGPT, Claude       | Server-to-client streaming (AI responses)     |
| **WebSockets**        | Slack, Instagram      | Bidirectional real-time (chat, notifications) |
| **Fan-Out on Write**  | Instagram, Twitter    | Pre-compute feeds for fast reads              |
| **CQRS**              | Uber, Amazon          | Separate read/write at different scales       |
| **Event Sourcing**    | Stripe, Banking       | Audit trail, payment reliability              |
| **CDN Edge**          | Netflix, Amazon       | Serve static content from nearest location    |
| **Saga Pattern**      | Amazon, Uber          | Distributed transactions across services      |
| **Priority Queues**   | ChatGPT, Uber         | Paid users get faster service                 |
| **Multi-Tenancy**     | Slack, Notion         | B2B SaaS with workspace isolation             |
| **Chaos Engineering** | Netflix               | Test resilience by breaking things            |
| **Idempotency**       | Stripe                | Prevent duplicate operations                  |
| **Circuit Breaker**   | Netflix, Amazon       | Gracefully handle downstream failures         |
| **Sharding**          | Instagram, Slack      | Horizontal database scaling                   |

sections.title: Architecture Decision Checklist
sections.body:
When building your next scalable app, ask yourself:

1. **Data Model**: SQL, NoSQL, or both? (Module 3)
2. **Communication**: Sync (REST/gRPC) or Async (events/queues)? (Module 4)
3. **Scaling**: Horizontal (more servers) or Vertical (bigger server)? (Module 2)
4. **Caching**: What data is read-heavy? Cache it. (Module 4)
5. **Real-Time**: Do users need instant updates? WebSocket or SSE? (Module 4)
6. **Background Work**: What can be deferred? Use task queues. (Project 9)
7. **Multi-Tenant**: Are you building for one org or many? (Project 10)
8. **Failure**: What happens when a service goes down? Circuit breakers, retries. (Module 2)
9. **Deployment**: Containers? CI/CD? Health checks? (Module 5)
10. **Security**: Auth, rate limiting, input validation. Always. (Module 1)
